Averse

uh-VURSS -- Latin ab- ('away') plus vertere ('to turn'): literally turned away from something. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Averse is having a strong dislike of or opposition to something.

My grandfather is so averse to technology that he still refuses to carry a cell phone.

Worked Example

Offered a chance to double her savings on a risky stock, an investor shakes her head immediately and moves her money into a plain savings account instead.

That instinctive turning away from something disliked -- here, risk -- is exactly what averse describes. Unlike 'afraid,' which centers on fear, averse centers on settled dislike or opposition.

How Averse Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

reluctant

reluctant: hesitant and unwilling

opposed

opposed: actively against something

disinclined

disinclined: lacking the desire or willingness to do something

Antonyms

eager

eager: full of enthusiasm and desire

keen

keen: eagerly interested in something

How Strong Is It? — reluctant → averse → opposed

reluctant vs. averse

reluctant vs. averse: Reluctant is milder than averse -- a reluctant person hesitates but may still go along, while an averse person has a settled dislike that makes them resist altogether.

opposed vs. averse

opposed vs. averse: Opposed is stronger and more public than averse: averse describes an inner dislike or distaste, while opposed suggests actively taking a stand against something.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — a-

prefix — a-: away from (variant of Latin ab-)

root — -verse

root — -verse: to turn (from Latin vertere, past participle versus)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin aversus meant 'turned away,' from ab- ('away', worn down to a-) and vertere ('to turn') -- someone averse to a thing has mentally turned away from it, the same root that gives us reverse and this unit's avert.

Root Check

Word Choice

Averse is almost always followed by 'to,' as in 'averse to risk' or 'not averse to a little adventure.' Take care not to confuse it with adverse, which means unfavorable, as in 'adverse weather.'
